title: AST parsing pipelines: lexer, parser, and error recovery
markdown:
## Why this matters

Every formatter, linter, bundler, and IDE feature is an AST pipeline. Lexer/parser design choices determine error quality, incremental speed, and refactor safety.

## The simple version

Reading code is like reading a sentence in two passes. First you chop it into words, that's the **lexer** turning raw characters into tokens (`function`, `(`, `x`, `)`, `{`). Then you figure out the grammar, that's the **parser** deciding those words form a function declaration, not just a pile of words in a row. A good parser is like a proofreader who, on hitting one bad sentence, doesn't throw out the whole page, they mark that one sentence as broken and keep reading, so spell-check still works on the rest of the document.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Source["raw source text"] --> Lexer[Lexer]
  Lexer --> Tokens["token stream: function, (, x, ), {"]
  Tokens --> Parser[Parser]
  Parser --> AST["AST (valid structure)"]
  Parser -.on error.-> ErrorNode["Error node (partial tree kept)"]
  ErrorNode --> AST
```

Where the analogy breaks: a human proofreader can use common sense to guess what a broken sentence probably meant. A parser's "error recovery" is much more mechanical, it typically just skips forward to the next token it recognizes as a safe restart point (a semicolon, a closing brace) and resumes from there, without understanding intent. That's why two syntax errors close together sometimes produce a confusing cascade of unrelated-looking diagnostics: the parser resynchronized at the wrong spot.

## Core mechanics

Lexer tokenizes with lookahead buffers. Parser builds an AST (often recursive descent) and may recover by synchronizing on tokens. Error nodes preserve partial trees for IDE services.

## Mental model

Parsing is streaming structure recognition: tokens are words, AST is syntax, diagnostics are UX.

## Runnable experiment

```js
// npm i @babel/parser
const { parse } = require('@babel/parser');

const brokenSource = 'function f(x { return x + 1; }'; // missing `)`
const ast = parse(brokenSource, { errorRecovery: true });
console.log(ast.errors.map((e) => `${e.reasonCode} @ ${e.loc.start.line}:${e.loc.start.column}`));
```

## Trade-offs and failure modes

Regex-based codemods ignore nesting and syntax entirely; they break the moment a pattern appears inside a string literal or comment. AST-based tools cost more upfront (you need a parser and a printer) but handle those cases by construction.

## Tool-building exercise

Build a 60-line CLI that parses a TS file and prints function declaration count plus first syntax error with line/column.

## Key takeaways

- Recovery keeps IDE features alive on broken code.
- Token lookahead defines lexer complexity.
- AST fidelity beats regex transforms.

exercise.title: Diagnose a syntax error with a real parser
exercise.instructions:
Create a tiny package, install `@babel/parser`, and parse three deliberately broken snippets: a missing closing paren, a missing closing brace, and an unterminated string. Compare fail-fast and recovery modes, then classify which later declarations remain usable. Finally, describe when an incremental concrete-syntax-tree parser such as Tree-sitter is a better fit.

Acceptance criteria: pin the parser and syntax plugins; print stable line/column diagnostics; preserve partial results where the parser supports them; test a string/comment false positive that a regex transform would corrupt; and document the parser/AST version as part of the tool's public contract.
exercise.deliverable: Printed error codes and positions for all three samples, plus one sentence on what the lexer had to guess for the unterminated string.
hints: errorRecovery: true is required or the parser throws instead of returning a partial tree.
The unterminated-string case usually forces the lexer to treat the rest of the file as part of the string until EOF or a recovery heuristic kicks in, that's worth noticing.
Compare the error node's reported position against where you'd point a human to fix it; they're often a token or two apart.

questions.prompt: Why do IDEs prefer error-recovering parsers?
questions.explanation: The misconception: assuming a syntax error should halt all tooling for the file. Like a proofreader marking one bad sentence and reading on, the parser keeps most of the tree intact so autocomplete and hover keep working around the broken spot.
questions.learning_objective: error recovery preserves a usable partial AST

questions.correct_answer: A stream of tokens with positions and kinds, consumed by the parser to build syntax structure.
questions.explanation: The misconception: conflating lexing with parsing as one step. Lexing is only the 'chop into words' pass, it has no idea what a valid sentence looks like; that grammar knowledge belongs entirely to the parser that consumes the token stream.
questions.learning_objective: lexing produces tokens; grammar structure is the parser's job

questions.explanation: The misconception: treating source code as flat text that pattern-matches safely. A regex has no concept of "inside a string" or "inside a comment" the way an AST does, so it matches text that merely looks right and breaks on real-world edge cases.
questions.learning_objective: regex text transforms ignore syntactic nesting that ASTs respect

questions.prompt: Which workload most strongly favors an incremental parser such as Tree-sitter?
choices: Recomputing syntax after every editor keystroke
Parsing one valid file once during a release
questions.correct_answer: Recomputing syntax after every editor keystroke
questions.explanation: The misconception is treating all parsers as interchangeable. An editor needs robust partial trees and cheap reuse after small edits, which is the workload incremental parsing is designed to serve.
questions.learning_objective: choose incremental parsing for repeated small edits and interactive tooling

questions.prompt: You are publishing a codemod across a monorepo with mixed syntax versions. Define the parser contract and rollout evidence needed before rewriting files.
questions.correct_answer: Pin parser and plugin versions, declare supported file extensions and syntax, reject or report recovery/error nodes, preserve comments and formatting through a tested printer, run idempotence and fixture tests, start in dry-run mode, and measure parse failures and diff size before staged writes.
questions.explanation: The misconception is considering a successful AST match sufficient. A production transform needs versioned syntax support, safe printing, deterministic behavior, diagnostics, and a reversible rollout.
questions.learning_objective: treat parser, AST, and printer behavior as a versioned codemod contract
